lesson.title: The Break-In That Brought Down a President
lesson.summary: A break-in at the Democratic National Committee headquarters in June 1972 unraveled into a sprawling scandal of abuse of power, illegal surveillance, and obstruction of justice that forced President Nixon to resign in August 1974, the only US president ever to do so.
lesson.body:
In the early morning hours of June 17, 1972, police arrested five men breaking into the Democratic National Committee offices at the Watergate office complex in Washington, DC, where they had planted wiretaps and were photographing documents. The burglars had ties to Nixon's reelection campaign, and although Nixon publicly denied any involvement and went on to win reelection that November in a landslide, evidence of a much wider conspiracy slowly emerged over the following two years.

Investigative reporters Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein of the Washington Post, aided by a source inside the FBI who used the pseudonym Deep Throat and was not publicly identified as associate FBI director Mark Felt until decades later, uncovered a pattern of White House efforts to cover up the break-in, including hush money payments to the burglars and misuse of federal agencies. Televised Senate Watergate Committee hearings in 1973 riveted the country, and a major breakthrough came in July 1973 when White House aide Alexander Butterfield revealed that Nixon had secretly recorded conversations in the Oval Office, creating a taped record of exactly what the president knew and when.

Nixon resisted turning over the tapes, claiming executive privilege, but the Supreme Court ruled unanimously in United States v. Nixon, decided in 1974, that he had to release them. One recording, from June 23, 1972, later known as the smoking gun tape, showed Nixon approving a plan to use the CIA to obstruct the FBI's investigation into the break-in just days after it happened, proof of the cover-up that even his remaining allies in Congress could not explain away.

With the House Judiciary Committee having already approved articles of impeachment and support collapsing even among Republican lawmakers, Nixon announced his resignation in a televised address on August 8, 1974, and left office the next day, becoming the only US president to resign. Vice President Gerald Ford, who had replaced Nixon's original vice president Spiro Agnew after a separate scandal, was sworn in as president and, weeks later, granted Nixon a full pardon. Watergate grew directly out of the same secretive, rule breaking culture within the Nixon White House that had produced the Plumbers unit after the Pentagon Papers leak, and it left a lasting legacy of public distrust in government along with reforms aimed at limiting future abuses of executive power.
